claims.text: The premelting and melting behavior of HEA nanoparticles is primarily controlled by nanoparticle–support interfacial strength.
Defective turbostratic graphite can provide a high-binding-energy interface for metallic nanoparticles.
Amorphous carbon can transform into highly defective turbostratic graphite during rapid high-temperature processing.
Nanoparticles can partially intercalate into and take root on turbostratic-graphite edge planes.
Intercalation and rooting on turbostratic-graphite edge planes produce high nanoparticle–support binding energy.
High nanoparticle–support binding energy strengthens nanoparticle anchoring and improves thermal stability.
Strong nanoparticle–support binding reduces the mobility or liquefaction of nanoparticle surface atoms.
Elevated interfacial binding energy opposes size-induced surface-melting depression.
Strongly supported HEA nanoparticles will have a higher measured melting temperature than otherwise identical unsupported or weakly supported nanoparticles.
Unsupported or weakly interacting HEA nanoparticles melt at lower temperatures because of enhanced surface-atom mobility and high surface-to-volume ratio.
The proposed support-induced shift in premelting and melting behavior should occur for HEA nanoparticles between approximately 5 and 20 nm.
Quantum effects may override the support-interaction mechanism for particles much smaller than 5 nm.
Factors other than support interaction may dominate melting behavior in bulk materials.
The magnitude of the melting-temperature increase varies with alloy composition, support defect density, and processing parameters.
Failure to observe a statistically significant premelting delay or melting-temperature increase on the high-binding support relative to the inert-support control would falsify the hypothesis.
